title: Thermodynamics
tagline: Properties of pure substances, energy balances for closed systems and control volumes, the second law, entropy and exergy, power cycles, mixtures and combustion
summary: Thermodynamics governs every engine, power station, refrigerator and compressor. The course develops the properties of pure substances and ideal gases, energy balances on closed systems and control volumes, the second law, entropy and exergy, and applies them to gas and vapour power cycles, ideal-gas mixtures and combustion.
overview: Thermodynamics is an accounting discipline. It opens with one law that says energy is conserved and a second that says it cannot all be used, and it spends the rest of the subject being exact about the difference between the two — first by learning what a quantity of matter can store, then by balancing what crosses a boundary, then by charging for what is destroyed on the way.

The course is built around the two things that make the subject hard for beginners: the fact that the properties you need are almost never available from a formula, so they are looked up in a table and the skill is classification and not algebra; and the fact that the second law is not a second book-keeping rule but a statement about the **quality** of energy, which turns out to be the number that decides what a power plant, a refrigerator and a fuel cell can each be worth.

Everything is worked on real working fluids at real plant conditions — steam at 25 MPa and 600 C, carbon dioxide at 10 MPa, refrigerants near their critical point — because the shortcuts that are safe in the textbook are unsafe exactly where the interesting machines operate. The gas and vapour power cycles are then derived, compared and discounted, and the course closes on mixtures and combustion, where the composition changes and the accounting has to follow it.

Calculus is used but not relied on: partial derivatives appear in the derivation of the property relations and nowhere else, and every derived result is evaluated numerically on a real substance so that the reader can see what the approximation cost.
outcomes: Choose a system boundary and a sign convention, and write a closed-system or control-volume energy balance that accounts for every crossing

Classify the state of a pure substance, read the saturation, superheated and compressed-liquid tables, and decide when the ideal-gas model is admissible from the reduced state and the compressibility factor
Compute boundary, shaft, spring and electrical work for the standard quasi-equilibrium processes, and evaluate the polytropic approximation against a real measured curve
Apply conservation of mass and energy to nozzles, throttling devices, turbines, compressors, heat exchangers and unsteady filling and emptying, and justify every term retained or dropped
Apply the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements, the Carnot limit and the Clausius inequality, and compute entropy change and entropy generation for real processes
Compute reversible work, irreversibility, exergy and second-law efficiency for closed systems and control volumes, and locate where a machine destroys the most work

Analyse the Otto, Diesel, Brayton, Rankine and combined cycles with their real-component corrections, and evaluate gas mixtures and combustion stoichiometry, enthalpy of formation and adiabatic flame temperature

chapters.title: Systems, properties and energy
chapters.summary: Systems and control volumes, state and equilibrium, temperature and pressure, and energy transfer by work and heat.

chapters.title: Properties of pure substances
chapters.summary: Phases and phase changes, property tables and diagrams, and the ideal-gas equation of state.

chapters.title: The first law for closed systems
chapters.summary: Energy balances for closed systems, boundary work, and the specific heats of ideal gases, liquids and solids.

chapters.title: Mass and energy in control volumes
chapters.summary: Conservation of mass and energy for steady-flow devices — nozzles, turbines, compressors, valves and heat exchangers — and for unsteady filling and emptying.

chapters.title: The second law
chapters.summary: Heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps, the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements, reversibility and the Carnot cycle.

chapters.title: Entropy
chapters.summary: The Clausius inequality, entropy changes of substances, isentropic processes and efficiencies, and entropy generation.

chapters.title: Exergy
chapters.summary: Reversible work and irreversibility, second-law efficiency, and exergy balances for closed systems and control volumes.

chapters.title: Gas and vapour power cycles
chapters.summary: The Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles, the Rankine cycle with reheat and regeneration, and combined cycles.

chapters.title: Gas mixtures and combustion
chapters.summary: Ideal-gas mixtures, fuels and combustion reactions, enthalpy of formation, adiabatic flame temperature and an introduction to chemical equilibrium.

history.title: Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu
history.detail: Sadi Carnot analysed a fixed quantity of air confined in a cylinder with a movable piston and asked only how much work it could give — an idealised closed system and a reversible cycle, worked out while heat was still thought of as a conserved fluid. The book was little read until Clapeyron restated it in 1834.

history.title: The mechanical equivalent of heat
history.detail: Joule's first value of the mechanical equivalent of heat, 838 ft·lbf per Btu (about 4.5 J/cal), came from electromagnetic experiments in 1843; his paddle-wheel experiments from 1845 gave 772 ft·lbf per Btu (about 4.16 J/cal, against today's 4.186) by 1850, and established that work and heat are interconvertible in a fixed ratio.

history.title: Two statements of the second law
history.detail: Clausius (1850, stated in its familiar form in 1854) held that heat does not of itself pass from a colder to a hotter body; Kelvin (1851) stated the impossibility of obtaining work from a cycle whose only effect is the cooling of a single reservoir. Each statement can be derived from the other.

history.title: The surface and the equation of state
history.detail: Gibbs's papers of 1873 gave a substance's properties a geometric representation (his memoir of 1875–78 added the phase rule and the general criteria of equilibrium); van der Waals's thesis of the same year gave an equation of state that reproduced a critical point and a two-phase region from a molecular model, and the dome became a drawn object.
history.people: Josiah Willard Gibbs, Johannes Diderik van der Waals

history.title: The property chart becomes an instrument
history.detail: Richard Mollier's enthalpy–entropy chart for steam, with the tables and diagrams that followed in 1906, turned the measured properties of steam into a tool that a turbine designer could read directly, and established the working method of looking a property up and knowing which region you are in.

history.title: IAPWS-95 and IF97
history.detail: The International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam adopted IAPWS-95 (1995), the reference equation of state for water for scientific use, and IAPWS-IF97 (1997), a faster industrial formulation that is the property basis of power-plant design and performance testing.
history.people: Wolfgang Wagner and the IAPWS working groups
